EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 16, 2026, gusty winds and snow squalls impacted eastern Nebraska. A shortwave trough pivoting across the Northern Plains drove an initial cold front and strong cold air advection (CAA) into the region. Behind a secondary cold front, enhanced atmospheric mixing tapped into higher winds aloft, transferring them to the surface. While widespread peak gusts ranged from 45 to 55 mph, isolated locations briefly recorded gusts of 58 to 62 mph. Additionally, horizontal convective rolls trailing the secondary front generated transient heavy snow showers, resulting in two distinct snow squalls. The intense winds within these bands caused localized blowing snow and rapidly reduced visibilities to 1/4 mile or less. The first squall moved through Cuming County during the late morning, followed by a second in Lancaster County during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow squall conditions impacted the county between 10:43 AM and 11:06 AM CST. KOAX radar indicated a robust convective band with high reflectivity moving rapidly through the area. During the passage of this band, various NDOT road cameras displayed near-zero visibility (under 1/4 mile).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 21, 2026, a shortwave disturbance moving across the northern Plains drove a cold front through eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Ahead of the frontal passage, northwesterly winds strengthened throughout the afternoon, driven by a tightening surface pressure gradient and deep mixing that tapped into stronger winds aloft. Consequently, strong, non-thunderstorm wind gusts overspread the region, with measured peak gusts ranging from 58 to 71 mph. Notable observations included 71 mph in Tekamah, NE, 64 mph near Verdel, NE, and 61 mph in Harlan, IA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 64 mph near Verdel, 60 mph near Creighton, and 58 mph near Bloomfield, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured at 1.50 inch in diameter. Photo of several 1.25 to 1.5 inch diameter stones.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Fire initiated southeast of Angora Nebraska in eastern Morrill County during the afternoon hours of March 12th. One direct fatality occurred as a result of the fire.

One primary residence was destroyed, along with 6 outbuildings damaged in the fire. Two calf-cow pairs were lost in the fire in Arthur County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 12, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. A surface low pressure system drifting across the U.S.-Canada border pushed an associated cold front through the region during the late afternoon hours, resulting in strong cold air advection behind the system. This thermal profile promoted deep boundary layer mixing, allowing localized areas to tap into a 55 to 70 knot flow aloft and transfer higher momentum to the surface. While much of eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa measured widespread wind gusts in the 48 to 56 mph range, localized deeper mixing produced higher localized gusts. Notably, a severe wind gust of 58 mph was recorded by the ASOS at the Tekamah Airport (KTQE) at 7:16 PM CST.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KTQE ASOS station measured wind gust of 58 mph at the Tekamah airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 15, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. During the morning hours, a deepening mid-level trough moved into the region and intensified an existing surface low pressure system. This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. This deep mixing tapped into a potent 60 to 70 knot jet descending on the backside of the system, efficiently transferring momentum to the surface and resulting in multiple measured wind gusts in the 58 to 64 mph range.||Additionally, the combination of snowfall and gusty winds reduced visibility to under a quarter mile for extended periods across portions of northeast Nebraska. Although snowfall totals peaked at just 3.5 inches in northern Cedar County, this was sufficient to produce several hours of blizzard conditions in the region. Further south, across the rest of eastern Nebraska, intermittent snow bands dropped 0.5 to 2 inches of snow, resulting in more sporadic reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: While no visibility observations were available within the county, surrounding counties measured several hours of visibility down to a quarter of a mile or less under snow and strong wind gusts. Wind gusts in the county were estimated in the 45-55 mph range with snowfall totals of 3-4 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northerly winds gusted as high as 50 mph near Emerson and 45 mph at South Sioux City. During and after a period of snow which totaled 1.5 inches at Emerson, visibility was reduced to one-quarter mile or less at times with blowing snow.

Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northerly winds gusted as high as 50 mph near Concord and near Emerson. During and after a period of snow which totaled 2.5 inches 3 miles northwest of Wakefield, 2.0 inches at Concord, and 1.5 inches at Newcastle, visibility was reduced to one-quarter mile or less at times with blowing snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 15, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. During the morning hours, a deepening mid-level trough moved into the region and intensified an existing surface low pressure system. This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. This deep mixing tapped into a potent 60 to 70 knot jet descending on the backside of the system, efficiently transferring momentum to the surface and resulting in multiple measured wind gusts in the 58 to 64 mph range.||Additionally, the combination of snowfall and gusty winds reduced visibility to under a quarter mile for extended periods across portions of northeast Nebraska. Although snowfall totals peaked at just 3.5 inches in northern Cedar County, this was sufficient to produce several hours of blizzard conditions in the region. Further south, across the rest of eastern Nebraska, intermittent snow bands dropped 0.5 to 2 inches of snow, resulting in more sporadic reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KLNK ASOS measured wind gust of 60 mph at the Lincoln Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured at 1.25 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning and afternoon hours of April 15th, 2026, an upper-level wave ejected northward into the central Plains, pushing an attendant surface low pressure system from southeast Nebraska northeastward into central Iowa. This system pulled a warm sector northward into eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa, interacting with a weak convergent boundary draped generally along and just north of the Interstate 80 corridor. Driven by afternoon high temperatures peaking in the 70s, instability increased through the day, with a narrow ribbon of surface-based CAPE (SBCAPE) values exceeding 2,500 J/kg wrapping into the mid-Missouri River Valley. Under the influence of this unstable and highly sheared environment, two elevated severe supercells tracked across eastern Nebraska into southwest Iowa.||The first severe cell tracked generally from Schuyler, Nebraska, east-northeastward into Dunlap, Iowa. This storm produced several reports of quarter-sized (one inch in diameter) hail along its track. As the storm moved through Harrison County, Iowa, it intensified further, producing golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) and wind-driven hail damage in Dunlap.||The second supercell developed northwest of Seward, Nebraska, and tracked northeastward to Wahoo, Nebraska, before gradually weakening as it approached the northern side of the Omaha metropolitan area. Notable severe reports from this storm included two-inch in diameter hail south-southwest of Dwight, Nebraska, and golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) within Dwight itself, which resulted in visual damage to residential vinyl siding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail estimated at 1.75 inches in diameter with lots of quarter sized hail mixed in. Hail caused damage to vinyl siding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured up to 1 inch in diameter near Lincoln, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Lincoln, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of April 25th, 2026, thunderstorms advancing into eastern Nebraska produced isolated pockets of large hail. This convection was driven by a cold front sweeping through the area. Ahead of the boundary, dewpoints rose into the mid-50s, supporting modest elevated instability (MUCAPE up to 1000 J/kg) alongside adequate deep-layer bulk shear. The first hail report was received around 4:56 PM CST near Seward, NE. Additional reports of hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter were received in Beatrice, NE, while a 1.75-inch hailstone was reported near Elk Creek, NE. Convective activity gradually decayed into the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured up to 1 inch in diameter near Seward, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wildfire started during the late morning hours of February 27th. By the time it was contained early that evening, a total of 1000 to 1200 acres of grassland was consumed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire started at the Otter Creek Ranch north northwest of highway 92 on the west end of Lake McConaughy. With gusty northwesterly winds, the fire tracked to the southeast leading to the evacuation of houses north of highway 92 in the Cedar View development. Firefighters were able to contain the fire before it reached those homes and the evacuation was lifted mid afternoon. A total of 1000 to 1200 acres of grassland was consumed by the fire. A total of 11 different fire departments battled the blaze.
